paper: Clark & West, Using out-of-sample MSPE to test the martingale difference hypothesis
what_it_establishes: Null is that the series is a ZERO MEAN martingale difference; benchmark is the 'no change' (zero) forecast. Under that null the population MSPE of the no-change model equals the linear alternative's, but the alternative's SAMPLE MSPE is larger; proposes the MSPE-adjusted statistic.
relation_to_this_project: This is the exact test our study runs. Decisive: the zero benchmark's null explicitly INCLUDES zero mean. With a nonzero drift the null is false, so rejection is correct behaviour of the test, not a defect of it.
verification_level: Abstract text read via search result; full PDF would not parse
verdict_for_our_novelty: KILLS the framing 'the standard test is broken'. Our 14-22% is the test correctly rejecting a null that applied users did not intend. The error is interpretive, not econometric.

paper: Clark & West, Approximately normal tests for equal predictive accuracy in nested models
what_it_establishes: General nested case. States that with standard normal critical values actual size is close to but a little BELOW nominal: one-sided at 1.645 gives size between .01 and .05.
relation_to_this_project: Our measured 5.3-6.2% against the recursive mean is roughly consistent with this (mildly above). Our 14-22% against zero is far outside it.
verification_level: Size statement read verbatim in search results
verdict_for_our_novelty: SUPPORTS our measurement as a departure worth reporting, but the reference behaviour was already documented by the original authors.

paper: Pincheira, Hardy & Munoz, 'Go Wild for a While!': a new test for forecast evaluation in nested models
what_it_establishes: Introduces the Wild Clark-West (WCW) statistic. Documents that CW 'may present severe size distortions at long horizons'; WCW is well-sized at long horizons; CW retains a power edge.
relation_to_this_project: Directly pre-empts our h=7 finding (CW ~10% at nominal 5%) AND our recommendation to add bootstrap/randomisation inference on f_t.
verification_level: FULL TEXT READ 2026-08-03 via r.jina.ai text proxy; WCW statistic, phi grid {0.01,0.02,0.04}*sd(e_2), K-smoothing formula all extracted
verdict_for_our_novelty: KILLS the 'a dependence-robust alternative is needed' contribution -- it exists. But we implemented it (audit/scripts/wcw.py) and measured that it does not help in this regime, which is itself reportable: WCW repairs degeneracy, not benchmark misspecification.

paper: Magner & Hardy, Cryptocurrency Forecasting: More Evidence of the Meese-Rogoff Puzzle
what_it_establishes: Tests the random walk hypothesis on 13 major cryptocurrencies 2018-2022 with AR components and lagged BTC returns, using Wild Clark-West / ENC-t nested tests and rolling and recursive windows. Section 2: 'we compare the predictive ability of our models against a simple naive random walk process (we consider the first difference of the random walk, which is equivalent to a zero forecast (DRW) or constant forecast (RW))' -- BOTH benchmarks are reported, in separate columns of Tables 4-7. Reports models outperforming the benchmark in a majority of exercises.
relation_to_this_project: Same asset class, same test family, same benchmark question, overlapping period. Resolves the open question from the 2026-07-30 gate: they use BOTH the driftless (zero) and the drift-inclusive (constant/sample-mean) benchmark, and they already use WCW rather than plain CW.
verification_level: FULL TEXT READ 2026-08-03 via r.jina.ai text proxy (MDPI still returns HTTP 403 to direct requests)
verdict_for_our_novelty: DECISIVE AGAINST OUR NOVELTY. Reporting both benchmarks is established practice in crypto forecasting, not a correction we are introducing. Our benchmark section must be framed as a measurement of consequences on one pipeline, not as a prescription.

paper: Pincheira, Hardy & Bentancor, A Simple Out-of-Sample Test of Predictability against the Random Walk Benchmark
what_it_establishes: A simple excess-profitability (SEP) out-of-sample test of the random walk hypothesis for the particular case in which the benchmark is a zero-mean forecast; motivated by directional/trading loss rather than MSPE.
relation_to_this_project: Adjacent but different object: a new test statistic based on excess profitability, not a size calibration of CW-family tests. Does not moot our calibration measurement.
verification_level: Description and authorship verified 2026-08-03 from Magner & Hardy (2022) Section 4 and reference list; full text still 403
verdict_for_our_novelty: NOT DECISIVE. Confirms the area is well covered but leaves the ML-learner calibration question open.

paper: Moosa & Burns, The random walk as a forecasting benchmark: drift or no drift?
what_it_establishes: Argues there is no theoretical reason the driftless random walk dominates; it is an empirical question. Driftless wins on RMSE but loses on directional accuracy, magnitude-and-direction measures, and profitability. Time-varying drift does better still.
relation_to_this_project: Establishes that drift-vs-no-drift benchmark choice changes conclusions -- but for POINT FORECAST ACCURACY, not for the SIZE of a nested test.
verification_level: Abstract read via two independent sources
verdict_for_our_novelty: PARTIAL. The 'benchmark choice matters' point is published. The 'benchmark choice determines the size of the nested test' point is, so far, not found in this paper.

what_it_establishes: The recursively estimated historical mean is the standard benchmark for out-of-sample equity premium predictability, and the R2_OS is defined against it.
relation_to_this_project: Our project already uses this benchmark for R2_OS (study.py:28) while testing significance against zero. The 'correct' benchmark was therefore already in the codebase and already standard in the adjacent literature.
verification_level: Widely established; not re-verified in this pass
verdict_for_our_novelty: WEAKENS novelty further. Using the recursive mean is not a new prescription; it is what the equity premium literature has done for ~20 years.
